diagram.title: How ICT Supports Daily Work
diagram.subtitle: People use devices to create, store, and share information.

nodes.label: Need Information
nodes.text: A person wants to learn, work, or communicate.

nodes.label: Use ICT Device
nodes.text: A computer or phone is used to process information.

nodes.label: Store Data
nodes.text: Information is saved for future use.

nodes.label: Share and Communicate
nodes.text: Information is sent to others quickly.

summaryPoints: ICT combines information handling and communication.
Devices help people process, store, and share information.
ICT is used in education, business, and everyday life.

diagram.title: Main Hardware Groups
diagram.subtitle: A computer system is built from input, process, storage, and output parts.

nodes.label: Input
nodes.text: Keyboard, mouse, scanner

nodes.label: Processing
nodes.text: CPU handles instructions and calculations.

nodes.label: Storage
nodes.text: SSD or HDD keeps data for later use.

nodes.label: Output
nodes.text: Monitor, printer, speaker

summaryPoints: Hardware means the physical parts of the computer.
The CPU processes instructions from users and programs.
Input and output devices connect the user to the system.

diagram.title: Software Categories
diagram.subtitle: System software supports the computer, while application software supports the user.

nodes.label: Software
nodes.text: Instructions that tell hardware what to do.

nodes.label: System Software
nodes.text: Operating systems and utility tools manage the computer.

nodes.label: Application Software
nodes.text: Programs like word processors and spreadsheets solve tasks.

summaryPoints: Software is not physical; it is a set of instructions.
System software manages hardware and the platform.
Application software helps users perform specific work.

diagram.title: Operating System as the Manager
diagram.subtitle: The OS stands between hardware and user applications.

nodes.label: User
nodes.text: The user gives commands through a screen or interface.

nodes.label: Operating System
nodes.text: Controls memory, files, devices, and programs.

nodes.label: Applications
nodes.text: Programs run using services provided by the OS.

nodes.label: Hardware
nodes.text: CPU, storage, memory, and devices work under OS control.

summaryPoints: The operating system manages resources for both user and software.
It provides file handling, device control, and memory management.
Without an OS, application programs cannot run smoothly.

diagram.title: From Real-World Data to Bits
diagram.subtitle: Computers turn different media types into binary patterns.

nodes.label: Text
nodes.text: Letters become character codes.

nodes.label: Numbers
nodes.text: Values are represented digitally.

nodes.label: Binary Form
nodes.text: Everything is stored using 0s and 1s.

nodes.label: Images
nodes.text: Pictures become pixels and values.

nodes.label: Sound
nodes.text: Audio becomes digital samples.

summaryPoints: A bit is the smallest data unit.
Binary is the common internal language of digital systems.
Text, images, and sound are all encoded into binary.

diagram.title: Common Number Systems
diagram.subtitle: Different bases help humans and computers represent values.

nodes.label: Decimal
nodes.text: Base 10 uses digits 0 to 9.

nodes.label: Binary
nodes.text: Base 2 uses 0 and 1.

nodes.label: Octal
nodes.text: Base 8 uses digits 0 to 7.

nodes.label: Hexadecimal
nodes.text: Base 16 uses 0 to 9 and A to F.

nodes.label: Conversion
nodes.text: Values can be converted between systems.

summaryPoints: A number system is defined by its base.
Binary is used by computers because circuits have two states.
Hexadecimal is a compact human-friendly form of binary.

diagram.title: Logic Gates and Decisions
diagram.subtitle: Digital circuits use simple rules to create decisions from binary inputs.

nodes.label: Inputs
nodes.text: Binary values such as 0 and 1 enter the circuit.

nodes.label: Logic Gates
nodes.text: AND, OR, and NOT apply decision rules.

nodes.label: Output
nodes.text: The result is another binary value.

nodes.label: Truth Table
nodes.text: Shows all possible input-output combinations.

summaryPoints: Logic gates are the building blocks of digital logic.
Each gate produces an output using a defined rule.
Truth tables are used to study and compare gate behavior.

diagram.title: How a Network Connects Devices
diagram.subtitle: Devices share data and resources through a communication path.

nodes.label: Computer A
nodes.text: A student or office computer joins the network.

nodes.label: Router / Switch
nodes.text: Directs data to the right place.

nodes.label: Computer B
nodes.text: Another device receives or shares data.

nodes.label: Shared Resource
nodes.text: Printer, Internet access, or files

summaryPoints: Networks connect multiple devices so they can communicate.
Routers and switches help move data between connected points.
Networking reduces duplication by sharing resources.

diagram.title: Simple Internet and Email Flow
diagram.subtitle: Users search, browse, and exchange messages over the Internet.

nodes.label: User
nodes.text: A person types a website or email action.

nodes.label: Browser / Mail App
nodes.text: The application sends the request.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.text: The global network carries the request.

nodes.label: Website / Email Server
nodes.text: The service returns the page or message.

summaryPoints: A browser is used to access websites.
Email allows electronic messages and attachments to be sent.
Internet services depend on connected devices and servers.

diagram.title: Protecting Digital Information
diagram.subtitle: Safe behavior reduces the chance of attacks and data loss.

nodes.label: Threats
nodes.text: Phishing, malware, weak passwords

nodes.label: Smart User Actions
nodes.text: Strong passwords, careful clicks, regular updates

nodes.label: Protection
nodes.text: Safer devices, accounts, and personal data

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.text: Recovery is possible after damage or attack.

summaryPoints: Cyber security combines awareness, good habits, and technical protection.
Strong passwords and updates reduce common risks.
Backups help restore data after an attack or mistake.

diagram.title: Word Processing Workflow
diagram.subtitle: A document moves from typing to editing to final presentation.

nodes.label: Type Draft
nodes.text: Enter the first version of the document.

nodes.label: Edit Text
nodes.text: Correct mistakes and improve wording.

nodes.label: Format Layout
nodes.text: Adjust fonts, headings, spacing, and page setup.

nodes.label: Save or Print
nodes.text: Prepare the final clean document.

summaryPoints: Word processors are used to create and improve text documents.
Editing changes the content; formatting changes the appearance.
Tools like spell check and find/replace improve quality quickly.

diagram.title: Spreadsheet Data Flow
diagram.subtitle: Values enter cells, formulas process them, and results become summaries.

nodes.label: Cells
nodes.text: Rows and columns hold values and labels.

nodes.label: Formulas / Functions
nodes.text: SUM and other functions calculate results.

nodes.label: Results
nodes.text: Totals, averages, and patterns appear.

nodes.label: Charts and Reports
nodes.text: Data can be visualized for decisions.

summaryPoints: Spreadsheets organize data in a grid.
Formulas automate repeated calculations.
Charts turn raw values into a quick visual summary.

diagram.title: How a Database Organizes Information
diagram.subtitle: Related data is stored in fields and records inside tables.

nodes.label: Fields
nodes.text: Each field stores one attribute like Name or Age.

nodes.label: Records
nodes.text: A row combines fields for one item or person.

nodes.label: Tables
nodes.text: Many records are stored together in a table.

nodes.label: Queries
nodes.text: Search conditions retrieve the exact data needed.

summaryPoints: Databases store structured data more effectively than plain lists.
Fields describe attributes, while records describe whole items.
Queries help users find useful data quickly.

diagram.title: Basic Program Logic
diagram.subtitle: Programs take input, process it, and produce output.

nodes.label: Input
nodes.text: The program receives data from the user or device.

nodes.label: Variables
nodes.text: Data is stored under meaningful names.

nodes.label: Logic
nodes.text: Sequence, selection, and repetition control actions.

nodes.label: Output
nodes.text: The program displays or returns a result.

summaryPoints: Variables hold data for later use in the program.
Selection helps a program choose between alternatives.
Repetition runs the same block of logic multiple times.

diagram.title: Problem Solving with Flowcharts
diagram.subtitle: An algorithm can be written as clear steps and visualized with symbols.

nodes.label: Start / End
nodes.text: The algorithm begins and finishes at clear points.

nodes.label: Process Step
nodes.text: A rectangle shows an action to perform.

nodes.label: Decision
nodes.text: A diamond checks a condition and branches.

nodes.label: Flow
nodes.text: Arrows show the order of steps.

summaryPoints: An algorithm is a step-by-step solution to a problem.
Flowcharts make logic easier to understand before coding.
Each symbol has a standard meaning in the flowchart.
